title: The AI Hub Weekly: Google’s Gemini Gets Faster, Cheaper, and Smarter
excerpt: Welcome back to another week of action in AI. The products that power our work, imagination, and daily lives keep getting upgrades—sometimes in ways we barely notice, sometimes in dramatic jumps.…
contentHtml:
Welcome back to another week of action in AI. The products that power our work, imagination, and daily lives keep getting upgrades—sometimes in ways we barely notice, sometimes in dramatic jumps. This time, the story is clear: AI models are getting not just smarter, but more accessible, affordable, and—crucially—practical.

TOP STORIES

Google’s Gemini Gets a Major Upgrade: Faster, Cheaper, and Now Makes Videos

  • Google launched Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, now generally available for business and developers.
  • The update introduces 15-second video creation, lets you edit conversations across multiple turns, and adds smarter referencing of previous context.
  • Pricing drops 30% from the previous version, with immediate effect; available through Gemini API and business plans.
  • Source

OpenAI and Hacktron Partner to Hunt for AI System Vulnerabilities

  • OpenAI announced a partnership with Hacktron to proactively test and find security weaknesses in its AI systems.
  • The effort focuses especially on connections to third-party apps and plug-ins, aiming to secure “frontier” AI.
  • Security researchers and hackers will play a direct role in making systems safer; expect public bug bounties and findings over coming months.
  • Source

OpenAI Benchmarks How Well AI Agents Do Real-World Science Tasks

  • OpenAI released BioBasicsBench, a set of 100 tasks to measure how AI agents interpret raw experimental data in everyday scientific (“wet-lab”) work.
  • The benchmark tests practical lab skills, not just theoretical knowledge, pushing agent capabilities closer to helping with real research.
  • This move hints at the direction AI assistants could take—doing real science, faster, and alongside humans.
  • Source

Australian Universities Roll Out AI-Native Curriculums for All Students

  • Australian universities are integrating ChatGPT access and AI-powered tools into teaching and learning at scale.
  • The goal: ensure every graduate is proficient using AI in schoolwork and future jobs, closing the global skills gap.
  • This change applies now and could reshape how degrees are viewed globally; expect other countries to watch and follow.
  • Source

OpenAI Unveils GPT‑6 Cyber, an AI Security Model That Finds Bugs and Fixes Them

  • GPT‑6 Cyber is a new specialized AI model aimed at cybersecurity, designed to autonomously find vulnerabilities and generate fixes in software.
  • The model was trained with strict guardrails to avoid misuse, staying within authorized contexts and attack boundaries.
  • Intended for security teams, developers, and ethical hackers; no consumer pricing yet, but signals a shift toward self-securing AI systems.
  • Source

Merge Builds Business Tools With OpenAI: AI Now Plans Dinners, Writes Sales Reports

  • The company Merge now uses OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex to automate everything from code reviews to marketing emails—and even plans executive dinners.
  • Shows how operational teams are deploying AI directly in non-technical business processes—not just ‘tech companies’ benefiting.
  • Highlights a bigger trend: if your workflow is digital, odds are AI can now assist somewhere in the chain.
  • Source

THIS WEEK IN AI

Every once in a while, we get a week where the future gets more evenly distributed. This is one of those weeks. The headline-grabbing upgrades—the new Gemini model that’s both faster and friendlier on your budget, the rise of video as a core AI skill, and cybersecurity bots that don’t just detect threats but fix them—signal a decisive move toward AI as an accessible, everyday utility. “AI for everyone” is becoming less of a slogan and more of a feature baked right into the products you (or your company) can actually use today.

The tension now is less about “will AI change our lives” and more about “who will keep up.” We’re seeing universities build AI fluency into their DNA, betting that a future graduate simply can’t compete without practical, hands-on experience using these tools—from essay-writing to data analysis. Meanwhile, the bleeding edge is already showing up at work: companies like Merge are letting AI plan the dinner, not just write the meeting notes, and security teams are eyeing GPT-6 Cyber as an always-on code reviewer and vulnerability hunter.

But with power comes risk. This week’s emphasis on vulnerability hunting—by both friendly hackers (hacktron) and the AI models themselves—tells us the stakes are high. As more organizations plug AI into everything from finance to building management, any exploit could have real-world consequences. There’s a quiet arms race between the people (and bots) who defend these tools and those looking to break them, for profit or just for the thrill.

So: what do we do with all this? First, if you work or study anywhere with access to these upgraded AI tools, this is the week to try what they can do for you. Ask yourself: which part of your workflow is repetitive, slow, or just plain dull? The right AI—now faster and cheaper than last month—might be able to handle it, or at least help.

And second, the challenge is to not get complacent as the tools get “easier.” There’s as much danger as opportunity wherever AI becomes invisible. Whose values shape what a “safe” AI model can or can’t do? Are we training every college student to be an AI-native—and what happens to those left out, whether in the classroom, the office, or the broader public?

For this week: push a little. Try something new with your favorite AI tool. And then, ask yourself: what would it take for this to stop feeling like magic, and start feeling like plumbing you rely on every day? Because that’s where we’re headed, fast.

MORE TOP STORIES

Flipsnack Lowers Cost per Signup Using AI-Boosted Ads

  • Flipsnack used ChatGPT-powered advertising campaigns to increase product signups while decreasing the cost for each new user.
  • The focus was on getting people to actually try the product, not just look at an ad, showing AI’s role in real business growth.
  • Case in point: AI-driven marketing is having a direct, measurable impact on bottom lines.
  • Source

Franklin Templeton Deploys OpenAI for Investment Research

  • Financial firm Franklin Templeton is rolling out OpenAI-powered workflows to help portfolio managers compare research and assess investment risks.
  • Starts with equity research, hinting at AI’s increasing role in analysis-heavy (and high-stakes) industries.
  • Financial pros, take note: the AI is coming for the footnotes, not just the headlines.
  • Source

OpenAI Acquires Pierre Computer Company to Supercharge AI Coding Tools

  • OpenAI announced its acquisition of Pierre Computer Company, aiming to improve Codex—the AI that helps people understand, write, and review code.
  • Directly signals a ramp-up in AI tools for building and managing software, especially for anyone who codes for a living.
  • Watch for faster updates and new features rolling out to developers and businesses soon.
  • Source

OpenAI Images 2.6: Faster Image Generation and New GIF Features

  • OpenAI released Images 2.6 with faster image creation, new GIF output options, and better photo editing control.
  • These upgrades are now available in ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI API.
  • Expect richer visual content and new creative workflows—especially for marketers, designers, and anyone who makes content for the web.
  • Source

DevRev Uses GPT-6.1 Sol for Self-Serve Enterprise Support

  • DevRev integrates GPT-6.1 Sol to power computer and operator roles, aiming for a balance of fast reasoning and cost efficiency in enterprise customer service.
  • Businesses now deploy AI not just as a chatbot, but as an autonomous helpdesk agent.
  • This marks yet another step toward AI replacing legacy support tools in big organizations.
  • Source

OpenAI Pushes Into Engineering: CAD, PCB Design, and More Go Digital

  • OpenAI is showcasing how ChatGPT and Codex are speeding up engineering work—from computer-aided design (CAD) to printed circuit board (PCB) layouts and simulations.
  • Engineers in “the physical world” are seeing AI move from theory to practical assistance in complex, technical workflows.
  • If you work in product design, expect AI to become as necessary as your CAD software.
  • Source
